title: Marrow hypercellularity is common and clinically neutral in essential thrombocythemia
Combating CD24 to overcome CD19 CAR-T resistance via induction of innate and adaptive immunity in B-cell malignancies
abstract: Abstract CD24 is highly expressed in aggressive B-cell malignancies and represents a novel immunologic vulnerability to overcome resistance to CD19 chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy. We developed a CD24 × CD3 bispecific antibody (CD24 BsAb) and CXCR3-armed CD24 CAR-T cells, both exhibiting potent antitumor activity in lymphoma and leukemia models. CD24 BsAb and CD24 CAR-T overcome CD19 CAR-T resistance driven by antigen loss and apoptosis defects in vitro and in vivo. Beyond direct cytotoxicity, CD24-targeted T cells reprogram macrophages toward an M1-like phenotype and enhance phagocytic clearance. We further engineered a dual-specific, dual-functional CD19 CAR-T that secretes a CD24 bispecific T-cell engager (CD24 BiTE), enabling simultaneous targeting of CD19 and CD24 to address tumor heterogeneity and achieve superior efficacy. Collectively, our study demonstrates that CD24-directed adoptive T-cell therapies are warranted for B-cell malignancies through robust induction of both innate and adaptive immune responses.

title: PHI-101: a novel FLT3 inhibitor with potent activity against the F691L gatekeeper resistance mutation
abstract: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a highly aggressive hematologic malignancy characterized by myeloproliferation, a block in differentiation, and accumulation of immature blasts in the bone marrow and peripheral blood [ 1 , 2 ]. The pathogenesis of AML is genetically diverse, with recurrent chromosomal and molecular alterations that drive leukemogenesis and influence prognosis and treatment decisions [ 1 , 2 ]. Mutations in the FMS-like tyrosine kinase 3 (FLT3) gene are among the most prevalent in AML and are strongly associated with relapse and reduced survival. Internal tandem duplication (ITD) mutations of the juxtamembrane region are the most common along with point mutations in the tyrosine kinase domain (FLT3-TKD), with both promoting constitutive kinase activity, albeit with distinct downstream effects [ 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 ]. FLT3 mutations have therefore become important therapeutic targets, leading to the development of small-molecule tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) [ 8 ].

title: Inhibition of PHB2/PINK1-mediated mitophagy potentiates venetoclax activity in acute myeloid leukemia
abstract: Abstract Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) cells are highly dependent on mitochondrial activity for survival, with this metabolic reliance driven in part by BCL-2, which is therapeutically targeted by venetoclax-based therapies. The regulation of mitochondrial dynamics in leukemic cells is therefore essential for maintaining mitochondrial homeostasis. However, the mechanisms that enable selective degradation of damaged mitochondria (mitophagy) are still poorly understood in AML. In this study, we sought to elucidate the role of PTEN-induced putative kinase 1 (PINK1), a key sensor of mitochondrial stress, in regulating mitophagy in leukemic cells. Our results identified PINK1 as a central modulator of mitophagy. Genetic depletion of PINK1 reduced both basal and stress-induced mitophagy, leading to mitochondria accumulation and functional impairment. Additionally, we discovered that PINK1 stabilization during mitochondrial stress is regulated by Prohibitin 2 (PHB2), and that depletion or inhibition of PHB2 mirrored the biological effects of PINK1 loss. Notably, both genetic depletion of PINK1 or PHB2, as well as pharmacological inhibition of PHB2, significantly increased AML cell sensitivity to venetoclax both in vitro and in vivo. Together, these findings highlight the potential of targeting the PHB2/PINK1 signalling pathway to improve the efficacy of venetoclax-based therapies in AML by disrupting the mitophagy process.

title: Fibroblast growth factor receptor-signaling confers stroma-mediated drug resistance in malignant B cells
Neoantigenic receptor ROR1 promotes cell growth through diverse and complementary mechanisms
abstract: Aberrant expression of neoantigenic receptor ROR1 has been identified in diverse lymphomas, including mantle cell lymphoma (MCL) and in a broad spectrum of nonlymphoid malignancies. While ROR1 has emerged as an attractive therapeutic target, its oncogenic role and the underlying mechanisms remain rather poorly characterized. Focusing on MCL, we found that ROR1 expression is heterogeneous and it can be induced under environmental stress. Inhibition of ROR1 expression resulted in cell-cycle suppression and apoptotic cell death. The ROR1 loss affected expression of numerous genes and altered phosphorylation of many proteins, including those involved in cell-cycle progression. ROR1 also promotes the synthesis of pyrimidines and purines, including induction of phosphorylation of enzymes involved in pyrimidine synthesis. Finally, we found that ROR1 induced phosphorylation of DEK and that its depletion abrogates ROR1 expression. These results provide insights into the multi-faceted oncogenic role of ROR1, further justifying targeting ROR1 in MCL and other malignancies.

title: Targeting the eIF4F translation initiation complex disrupts BCR::ABL1 translation and overcomes drug resistance in CML
abstract: Chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) is driven by the constitutively active BCR::ABL1 kinase, which promotes uncontrolled cell proliferation. Although protein-tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) have revolutionized CML treatment, resistance remains a significant barrier to curative therapy, particularly due to BCR::ABL1 mutations and the persistence of leukemia stem cells (LSCs). New treatment strategies that directly inhibit BCR::ABL1 protein expression are needed to achieve more effective therapy. Using a high-content antibody microarray and bioinformatics analyses, we investigated differences in the proteome and phosphorylation landscape of Imatinib (IM)-resistant cells and identified highly activated members of the eukaryotic translation initiation complex (eIF4F), particularly eIF4G1, a core component of eIF4F. These eIF4F complex members are highly expressed and activated in CD34 + CML stem/progenitor cells and in IM-resistant cells. Genetic inhibition of eIF4G1 or pharmacological targeting with the small-molecule inhibitor SBI-756 diminished eIF4F complex assembly, reduced overall translation initiation, reduced BCR::ABL1 expression and key downstream targets, impaired the survival of nonresponder stem/progenitor cells, including BCR::ABL1-T315I mutant cells, and sensitized them to TKIs, with strong synergistic effects in vitro and in a PDX model. These findings underscore the potential of eIF4F complex inhibition as a new therapeutic strategy to overcome TKI resistance in CML and other BCR::ABL1 + malignancies.

title: Correction: Clinical and transcriptomic characterization of patients with chronic lymphocytic leukemia harboring t(14;19): an ERIC study
abstract: In this article, the author’s name was incorrectly written as Arnon Kater (Kater A). The correct name should be Arnon P Kater (Kater AP). The original article has been corrected.

title: Targeting the mitochondrial complex I subunit NDUFS2 potentiates FLT3 inhibition in acute myeloid leukaemia with FLT3 internal tandem duplication
abstract: Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) with FLT3 internal tandem duplication (FLT3-ITD) frequently relapses after FLT3 tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapy, highlighting the need to define mechanisms of drug tolerance. Here, we identify the mitochondrial complex I core subunit NDUFS2 as a determinant of FLT3 TKI tolerance in FLT3-ITD AML. A metabolism-focused CRISPR-Cas9 sensitiser screen, integrated with transcriptomic profiling of gilteritinib-resistant cells and primary samples, identified NDUFS2 as upregulated in acquired resistance and preferentially expressed in FLT3-ITD AML. NDUFS2 knockdown impaired complex I activity, oxidative phosphorylation, mitochondrial membrane potential and ATP production, thereby promoting apoptosis and sensitising FLT3-ITD AML cells to gilteritinib. Pharmacologic complex I inhibition with IACS-010759 similarly enhanced gilteritinib activity in FLT3-ITD AML cell lines and primary FLT3-ITD samples, activated AMPK-PERK-ATF4-CHOP stress signalling, promoted apoptosis, and reduced leukaemia burden in a patient-derived xenograft model. Genetic NDUFS2 knockdown also prolonged survival in a xenograft model. A preliminary murine safety assessment showed no overt toxicity under the tested short-term dosing schedule. These findings identify NDUFS2-dependent complex I activity as an adaptive metabolic dependency supporting FLT3 inhibitor tolerance and provide mechanistic insight for further preclinical evaluation.

title: Predicting long-term survival in primary myelofibrosis
abstract: We interrogated data from 217 subjects with primary myelofibrosis (PMF) diagnosed before 2001 to identify covariates at diagnosis associated with long-term survival. Forty-one survived more than 25 years. Long-term survivors were more often female, younger than 50 years and less likely to have anemia, splenomegaly, increased blood CD34-positive cells, a JAK2 V617F variant, and more likely to have grade-0 bone marrow fibrosis and increased platelets. In multivariable logistic regression analyses, age <50 years, platelet count >450 × 10⁹/L, and grade-0 bone marrow fibrosis independently predicted long-term survival. These co-variate associations were confirmed in Cox regression with landmark analyses. Long-term survivors had a lower cumulative incidence of anemia and thrombocytopenia during follow-up. Identifying long-term survivors at diagnosis provides clinically meaningful prognostic information in PMF and may influence therapy decisions.

title: Multiple myeloma in the Netherlands: 35-year trends in incidence and survival
authors: Catharina H. M. J. van Elssen
Niels W. C. J. van de Donk
abstract: Multiple myeloma (MM) has an incidence of 4.5–6.0 per 100,000 individuals and a median age at diagnosis of 70 years in Europe [ 1 ]. The treatment of MM has advanced rapidly over the past decades, translating into substantial overall survival (OS) improvements [ 1 , 2 ].

title: Concordance between bone marrow and blood measurable residual disease after first-line novel agent treatment for chronic lymphocytic leukemia: a systematic review and meta-analysis
Serine auxotrophy is a targetable vulnerability driven by PSAT1 suppression in AML
abstract: Serine metabolism is of growing biologic and therapeutic interest in cancer. Upregulation of the serine synthesis pathway (SSP) can fuel tumor growth, and cancers with this phenotype are often sensitive to. SSP inhibitors. In parallel, dietary restriction of serine and glycine (SG) can suppress some cancers, but the determinants of sensitivity to. this approach are poorly understood. This is especially true in acute myeloid leukemia (AML), where serine metabolism has been less explored. We report that a subset of human AML cell lines and primary samples are completely dependent on external serine, known as serine auxotrophy. These leukemias consistently suppressed the SSP enzyme PSAT1, failed to. synthesize serine, responded to. SG restriction in vivo, and were rescued by restoring PSAT1. We also found that SG restriction synergized with venetoclax in serine auxotrophic AML, and that MECOM rearrangement was strongly associated with PSAT1 suppression and serine auxotrophy. These findings define a metabolically distinct AML subtype and nominate it for targeting by SG restriction.

title: Rapid proteasomal degradation of mutant feline McDonough sarcoma-like tyrosine kinase-3 overcomes inhibitor resistance mechanisms of acute myeloid leukemia cells
abstract: Abstract The hyperactive kinase FLT3-ITD causes acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and is a prognostic biomarker. We synthesized and characterized MA191 as a novel von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) E3 ubiquitin ligase-based proteolysis targeting chimera (PROTAC) for FLT3. MA191 induces apoptosis in cultured and primary AML patient cells harboring FLT3-ITD (IC 50 =9.6-11 nM; EC 50 =0.001-0.883 µM). Comparison with a VHL-binding-deficient stereoisomer of MA191 demonstrates that FLT3-ITD degradation is superior to kinase inhibition ( p < 0.03). Rapid depletion of FLT3-ITD by MA191 (DC 50 =10 nM) requires VHL, neddylation, proteasome activity, and the pro-apoptotic BH3-only protein BIM. MA191 reduces FLT3-ITD prior to apoptosis, uncovering apoptosis-independent roles of BIM for protein stability. Higher expression levels of FLT3 in leukemia cells than in healthy cells ( n = 3675/ n = 1249) are associated with worse AML patient survival ( p = 0.0099). MA191 does not harm healthy blood and bone marrow progenitor cells or myeloid cell differentiation. In Danio rerio larvae, MA191 halts AML cell proliferation without significant toxicity. Human stromal cell interactions and mutations in the tyrosine kinase domain of FLT3-ITD that confer resistance to FLT3 inhibitors do not abolish anti-leukemic effects of MA191. Accordingly, leukemia cells with acquired resistance to MA191 lack such mutations. We offer a framework for fast-acting next-generation FLT3 degraders that overcome resistance mechanisms to classical inhibitors.

title: Measurable residual disease is not a universally reliable surrogate for progression-free survival in clinical trials of new chronic lymphocytic leukemia therapies
Clinical and molecular characteristics of FLT3-ITD microclones in elderly patients with acute myeloid leukemia receiving less-intensive therapy
abstract: Internal tandem duplications (ITD) of the FMS-like Tyrosinkinase 3 ( FLT3 ) are detected in up to 30% of all newly diagnosed acute myeloid leukemia (AML) cases, with a decreasing prevalence in elderly patients [ 1 ]. FLT3 -ITD positivity in AML patients predicts poor prognosis and shorter median overall survival (OS), corresponding to an intermediate genetic risk classification per the ELN 2024 less-intensive score [ 2 ]. There are promising new studies examining triplet therapies combining hypomethylating agents (HMA), venetoclax and targeted FLT3 -inhibitors for unfit FLT3 -ITD positive patients [ 3 ]. Interestingly, FLT3-ITD microclones (defined by an allelic ratio (AR) < 0.05) have recently been detected in up to 25% of young AML patients considered fit for intensive chemotherapy who were classified as FLT3 -ITD negative by conventional fragment length analysis [ 4 , 5 , 6 ]. FLT3 -ITD microclones co-occur with NPM1 and DNMT3A mutations and have been linked to inferior relapse-free survival (RFS) as well as higher measurable residual disease (MRD) levels in younger patients with NPM1-mutated AML [ 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 ]. Currently, the incidence and prognostic impact of FLT3 -ITD microclones in elderly, unfit patients remain unclear. Given the prognostic relevance of FLT3 -ITD microclones in younger cohorts and its potential therapeutic implications, we sought to evaluate the impact of FLT3 -ITD microclones in elderly individuals. 201 AML patients aged ≥65 years at diagnosis were included in this study: patients received first-line less-intensive therapy or best supportive care (BSC) at our institution between 2006 and 2026 and were FLT3 -ITD negative in fragment length analysis at initial diagnosis with an AR < 0.05 (Supplementary Fig. S1 ). The median age at diagnosis was 76 years (range 65–90), and 125 patients were male (62%). 95 patients (47.3%) were treated with HMA-monotherapy, 67 patients (33.3%) with HMA plus combination therapy (+venetoclax [ n = 62]/ivosidenib [ n = 5]), 38 patients (18.9%) with best supportive care (BSC) only, and complete treatment data were not available for one patient (0.5%). Targeted ultrahigh-sensitivity error-corrected next-generation sequencing (NGS) and fragment length analysis by capillary electrophoresis was performed for all patients at initial diagnosis, as previously described [ 8 , 9 ]. The presence of FLT3 -ITD by NGS was analyzed with three different methods to enhance sensitivity and specificity, the open-source algorithms filt3r, getITD and a custom script [ 10 , 11 ]. NGS-based myeloid panel and cytogenetic analysis was conducted as described before [ 8 , 12 ]. The median sequencing depth of our ultrasensitive NGS-assay was 161.392 reads per sample (range 51.629–474.239). FLT3 -ITD microclones were detected in 21 out of 201 (10.4%) patients at initial diagnosis with a median VAF of 0.035% (range 0.007–1.153%) (Supplementary Fig. S2 ). 16 out of 21 patients (76.2%) harbored a single FLT3 -ITD insertion, two patients (9.5%) had two FLT3 -ITD insertions, and three patients (14.3%) had three to five FLT3 -ITD insertions. Insertion length ranged from 6 to 102 nucleotides, with a median insertion length of 33 nucleotides. When comparing the ultrahigh-sensitivity NGS results with fragment length analysis, only 6 of 21 (28.5%) FLT3 -ITD microclones identified by NGS were detected by fragment length analysis with an AR below 0.05. Notably, the FLT3 -ITD microclones detected by both methods showed a higher VAF with a median of 0.617% (range 0.023–1.153%), whereas the microclones missed by fragment analysis were smaller with a median VAF of 0.031% (range 0.007–0.293). Patients with FLT3 -ITD microclones demonstrated a significantly higher white blood cell (WBC) count at diagnosis compared to patients without FLT3 -ITD microclones (23.9 vs. 6.95 10^9/l, p = 0.027), whereas no difference was observed for hemoglobin (9 vs. 8.9 10^9/l, p = 0.517) and platelets (67 vs. 47.5 10^9/l, p = 0.502) (Table 1 ). We found no significant difference for age, sex and AML type. According to the ELN 2024 classification for patients receiving less-intensive therapy, patients with FLT3 -ITD microclones were more frequently classified as intermediate risk (38.1% vs. 17.2%) and less frequently as adverse risk (0% vs 25%) compared to patients without FLT3 -ITD microclones ( p = 0.019). Cytogenetic analysis revealed a trend toward a lower incidence of a complex aberrant karyotype in patients with FLT3 -ITD microclones compared to those without FLT3 -ITD microclones, although the difference was not statistically significant (4.8% vs 27.8%, p = 0.068). Evaluation of molecular co-mutations showed a trend toward a lower frequency of TP53 mutations in patients with FLT3 -ITD microclones (0% vs. 25.6%, p = 0.11). Furthermore, we did not detect a higher frequency of NPM1 mutations in the FLT3 -ITD microclone cohort (10% vs. 13.6%, p = 0.817). However, patients with FLT3 -ITD microclones showed a significantly higher prevalence of DNMT3A ( p = 0.02), SMC3 ( p = 0.02) and NRAS ( p = 0.03) mutations, as well as numerical increase in BCOR mutations ( n = 0.16) (Table 1 , Fig. 1A ) . Fig. 1: Genetic landscape and prognostic impact of FLT3 -ITD microclones. Full size image A Comparison of the mutational landscape between FLT3 -ITD microclone positive and negative patients. Myeloid panel data were missing for one FLT3 -ITD microclone-positive and four FLT3 -ITD microclone-negative patients. B Overall survival (OS) between FLT3 -ITD microclone positive and negative patients. Table 1 Baseline characteristics of elderly AML patients with or without FLT3 -ITD microclones. Full size table We next investigated the prognostic impact of FLT3 -ITD microclones in elderly AML patients receiving non-intensive therapy, particularly given that the current ELN risk classification for less-intensively treated patients considers FLT3 -ITD positivity as an adverse classifier. In the whole group, there was no difference in overall survival (OS) between patients with vs without FLT3 -ITD microclones ( p = 0.97) (Fig. 1B ). However, among patients receiving BSC only, those with FLT3- ITD microclones had a significantly shorter OS than FLT3 -ITD negative patients (HR 2.8, CI 1.006–7.808, p = 0.04) (Supplementary Fig. S3A ). This difference in OS was not observed in patients who received HMA-monotherapy ( p = 0.64) or HMA-based combination therapy ( p = 0.68) (Supplementary Fig. S3B –D). To characterize the clonal evolution of FLT3 -ITD microclones, available follow-up samples from 7 FLT3 -ITD microclone positive patents at different timepoints during treatment were analyzed (Supplemental Figs. S2 , S4 ). One Patient (patient 20) achieved complete remission after four cycles of azacitidine and venetoclax and lost the FLT3 -ITD microclone upon remission. Another patient (patient 15) showed re-emergence of peripheral blasts after two years of decitabine treatment and the FLT3 -ITD microclone clone expanded from 1.15 to 9.52%. Two patients harboring small FLT3 -ITD microclones of 0.029% (patient 8) and 0.0074% (patient 6) lost their microclones following refractory disease after one and 8 cycles of HMA monotherapy, whereas three other patients (patient 17, 16 and 14) with refractory disease showed an expansion of their FLT3 -ITD microclone after ≤4 cycles of HMA-based therapy. We next used ultrahigh-sensitivity NGS to evaluate whether patients initially assessed as FLT3 -ITD microclone negative acquired a FLT3 -ITD mutation at the time of relapsed or refractory (R/R) disease. Among 19 initially FLT3 -ITD microclone negative patients with available R/R samples, no detectable FLT3 -ITD mutations emerged during R/R disease. Taken together, our analysis using ultrahigh-sensitivity NGS detected FLT3 -ITD microclones in 10.4% of elderly AML patients receiving less-intensive therapy who were previously classified as FLT3 -ITD negative by conventional fragment length analysis. The proportion of patients with FLT3 -ITD microclones was lower than reported in younger, intensively treated patients, consistent with a lower prevalence of FLT3 -ITD mutations in elderly AML patients [ 1 ]. Fragment length analysis detected only 28.5% of these microclones, all at an AR < 0.05, reinforcing that NGS provides higher sensitivity for identifying small FLT3 -ITD clones. Compared with FLT3 -ITD-negative patients, elderly AML patients with FLT3 -ITD microclones tended to have a lower incidence of TP53 mutations and were less frequently classified as ELN adverse risk. Additionally, the lower prevalence of complex karyotypes in microclone-positive patients suggests a distinct biological background with a weaker association with secondary, pre-existing myeloid conditions than typically seen in elderly patients. Interestingly, we did not find an association between FLT3 -ITD microclones and NPM1 -mutations, although this association has been reported for FLT3 -ITD microclones in younger AML patients treated with intensive chemotherapy [ 5 , 6 ]. Nevertheless, the previously described co-occurrence with DNMT3A was also observed in our cohort of elderly FLT3 -ITD microclone-positive patients. In addition, we identified an association between FLT3 -ITD microclones and mutations in NRAS , another gene involved in signal transduction, that has not been described in younger AML patients. The higher WBC count at initial diagnosis and inferior OS in patients only receiving BSC suggest a more proliferative phenotype in elderly AML patients with FLT3 -ITD microclones, highlighting the proliferation-enhancing potential of even small FLT3 -ITD clones. However, HMA-based therapy appears to mitigate these OS disparities, suggesting that FLT3 -ITD microclones have less prognostic impact than macroclones, as reflected by the ELN2024 recommendations. Most FLT3 -ITD microclones persisted during R/R disease, with some showing clonal expansion, whereas microclones with a VAF < 0.1% were occasionally lost, even in refractory disease. None of the patients assessed as FLT3 -ITD negative by NGS at diagnosis acquired a FLT3 -ITD mutation at R/R disease, suggesting that FLT3 -ITD mutations at relapse mainly originate from pre-existing subclones. Our study is limited by the small number of patients with FLT3 -ITD microclones, reflecting the rarity of this subgroup, as well as by the limited number of patients treated with HMA plus venetoclax. Further studies in larger cohorts are required to better understand mechanisms of resistance and clonal evolution and to evaluate the potential role of FLT3 -ITD monitoring for early detection of treatment resistance in non-intensively treated patients with FLT3 -ITD microclones detected at diagnosis. The clinical implications of FLT3 -inhibitor therapy in patients with FLT3 -ITD microclones remain unclear. In younger patients with FLT3 -ITD mutations, the addition of FLT3 -inhibitors to intensive chemotherapy has been shown to improve outcomes regardless of AR and clone size [ 9 , 13 ]. Furthermore, the QUIWI-trial demonstrated superior outcomes with quizartinib treatment even among patients considered FLT3 -ITD negative [ 14 ]. A subsequent subgroup analysis revealed a non-significant trend toward longer remission duration with quizartinib in FLT3 -ITD microclone-positive patients [ 15 ]. In summary, our data shows that FLT3 -ITD microclones occur in a substantial proportion of elderly, unfit AML patients, represent a more proliferative type of AML and show a distinct mutational pattern. In our study, FLT3 -ITD microclones have no prognostic implications in elderly patients receiving standard therapy. However, larger studies are required to validate this finding and to clarify whether targeted combination therapies play a role in this patient population.

title: The cyclin-G associated kinase (GAK) is a clinically actionable drug target required for mitosis in diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
abstract: Abstract Though 100 kinase inhibitors are approved for clinical use, most kinases in the genome remain poorly characterized. Moreover, though kinase inhibitors have revolutionized the care of selected cancers, most others respond transiently or not at all to these drugs, typically directed against signal-transduction pathways. Given cellular regulation at every step by phosphorylation events, we hypothesized that phenotypic screening and machine-learning analysis can reveal novel kinase targets. Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL), the most common lymphoma, responds poorly to signal transduction-directed kinase inhibitors. We applied a library of probes to DLBCL systems broadly representing its pathogenic heterogeneity and subjected results to iterative target-deconvolution analysis aimed at tumor selectivity (idTRAX). These efforts identified the cyclin G-associated kinase (GAK) as a tumor-selective target. Mechanistic studies showed GAK kinase activity is required for mitotic progression, with inhibition leading to G2/M arrest and cell death and increased efficacy in the absence of the retinoblastoma (RB) tumor suppressor. GAK-directed kinase inhibitors, including repurposed clinical compounds, showed promising single-agent anti-DLBCL activity in vivo. GAK kinase function is therefore a targetable dependency, opening novel treatment strategies suitable for rapid clinical translation. Moreover, we establish phenotypic screening with target deconvolution as a generalizable strategy to reveal tumor-selective kinase dependencies.

title: Relcobatinib, a highly selective ATP-competitive ABL1 tyrosine kinase inhibitor for the treatment of chronic myeloid leukemia
abstract: Relcobatinib (ELVN-001) is a next-generation, investigational, BCR::ABL1 active-site tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) with a unique P-loop folded-in binding mode designed to deliver best-in-class efficacy with an improved tolerability profile over that of other TKIs for the treatment of chronic myeloid leukemia (CML). We demonstrate that relcobatinib has marked selectivity for BCR::ABL1, without inhibition of off-target kinases implicated in toxicities related to other TKIs. Relcobatinib exhibited greater selectivity than other active-site TKIs and demonstrated robust activity in vitro against native BCR::ABL1 and a broad range of clinically relevant TKI-resistant mutants. A BCR::ABL1 mouse xenograft model of human CML showed marked anti-tumor activity with relcobatinib as monotherapy, and, in combination with asciminib, showed further durable tumor regression, supporting the complementary mechanism of action between an active-site TKI and an allosteric inhibitor. Collectively, the preclinical profile of relcobatinib, marked by selective BCR::ABL1 targeting, supports its potential to improve efficacy and tolerability in the treatment of CML and other BCR::ABL1-driven malignancies, as monotherapy and in combination with an allosteric inhibitor.

title: Salvage therapy for immune-mediated bone marrow failure
abstract: Abstract Most acquired idiopathic bone marrow failure syndromes (BMFS) are thought to be cytotoxic T cell-mediated and are responsive to immunosuppressive therapies (IST) targeting T cells. However, in addition to frequent relapses, a proportion of cases remain refractory to first- and second-line agents due to a lack of clinical trials in the refractory and relapsed disease setting. Recently, the landscape of IST has expanded significantly, harnessing multiple molecular pathways that could be theoretically useful in the BMFS setting. In this manuscript, we retrospectively analyzed clinical responses to selected salvage IST, including sirolimus, tofacitinib, and subcutaneously administered abatacept and alemtuzumab, in a cohort of 151 patients with aplastic anemia, pure red cell aplasia, large granular lymphocytic leukemia, and other rare hypoproliferative BMFS. Our results indicate significant salvage rates with these agents and differential efficacy in specific clinical scenarios, showing differences in responses in affected lineages and in different disease states. We report that different modalities of IST may have lineage-restricted and overall responses in relapsed or refractory BMFS states, and durable response can be achieved in clinically difficult cases. These findings underscore the need for clinical trials to establish the safety and efficacy of alternative agents as substitute lines of therapy in BMFS.

title: Mutant calreticulin-driven myeloproliferative neoplasms favour the emergence of TIGIT-positive NK cells
abstract: Abstract Myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPNs) are chronic diseases characterized by an excessive production of myeloid blood cells. Janus kinase ( JAK2 ) V617F is the most common mutation in MPNs but a substantial proportion of patients harbour calreticulin ( CALR ) mutations—an attractive target for emerging immunotherapies. Natural killer (NK) cells have a central role in the elimination of malignant cells, but NK cells of MPN patients have reduced activity. Thus, reactivating their function might improve the disease outcome. Here, we demonstrate that NK cells from a CALR -mutant mouse model exhibit normal maturation but enhanced degranulation. Consistently, NK cells from CALR -mutant patients exhibit preserved degranulation ability, exceeding that observed in JAK2 -mutant patients. Notably, NK cells from CALR -, but not JAK2 -mutant patients express high levels of the immune checkpoint TIGIT possibly due to increased abundance of immunomodulatory proteins in the plasma. Moreover, CD34⁺ cells from MPN patients express elevated levels of the TIGIT ligand CD112. TIGIT blockade results in reduced platelet numbers in a transplant mouse model. These findings suggest that NK cells in CALR -mutant MPNs are activated but functionally constrained when encountering TIGIT ligand–expressing target cells, providing a strong rationale for exploring TIGIT blockade to restore NK-cell immunity in this disease subset.
